title: GDP base-year revision (2015) and the contested back-series
whatChanged: CSO moved the GDP base year from 2004-05 to 2011-12 in January 2015, adopting GVA and SNA 2008 methodology with MCA-21 corporate data. FY2013-14 growth reads 4.7% on the old base but 6.9% on the new. Two conflicting back-series followed in 2018: the NSC Mundle committee version (higher UPA growth, double-digit peaks) and the CSO/NITI Aayog version (lower UPA growth). Arvind Subramanian (2019) argued 2011-17 growth was overstated by ~2.5pp.
bridgeNote: No accepted reconciliation. Instrument policy: carry both series with a visible seam; never splice.

competingAccounts.position: Back-series lowers UPA-era growth; official position
Back-series shows higher UPA growth incl. double-digit years; shelved as 'experimental'
Post-2011 growth overstated ~2.5pp; actual ~4.5% vs official ~7% for 2011-17
Subramanian critique cherry-picked, not statistically robust

title: EUS to PLFS employment survey transition
whatChanged: NSSO Employment-Unemployment Survey (quinquennial, last round 2011-12) replaced by Periodic Labour Force Survey from 2017-18, with changed sampling design and stratification. Pre/post employment comparisons are methodologically contested; no official bridge estimates exist.

title: Withheld 2017-18 Consumer Expenditure Survey
whatChanged: The NSS 2017-18 Household Consumer Expenditure Survey was not released after leaked results indicated declining rural consumption; the government cited data-quality issues. Result: no official consumption-based poverty estimate after 2011-12 until the 2022-23 HCES (itself on a changed methodology).
bridgeNote: 2022-23 HCES uses a modified questionnaire and imputation approach; not comparable with 2011-12 without contested adjustments.

title: Census 2021 not conducted
whatChanged: The decennial census due 2021 was postponed (COVID cited) and has not been conducted as of the project's last update. Every per-capita and rate-based indicator after 2011 rests on population projections, with error compounding over time.

title: WPI-to-CPI inflation regime change
whatChanged: Headline inflation reference shifted from WPI to CPI (combined) around 2013-14; formal CPI inflation targeting (4% +/-2%) adopted 2016 via amended RBI Act. Long-run inflation narratives spanning the change must state which index they use.
bridgeNote: Both indices continue to be published; the break is interpretive, not a data gap.

title: Off-budget borrowing and fiscal accounting
whatChanged: Off-budget devices (FCI food-subsidy bonds, NSSF loans to public entities) understate the headline fiscal deficit in both eras. CAG flagged the practice; a partial clean-up brought FCI dues on-budget in FY2020-21, creating a one-year spike that is an accounting artefact, not a spending surge.
bridgeNote: CAG and budget documents allow partial reconstruction of extended deficit measures.
notes: Scope extended to banking: the Oct 2017 recapitalisation used ~₹1.35 lakh crore of recap bonds, which are the same off-budget device this record describes.

title: NCRB reporting changes and communal-violence data gaps
whatChanged: NCRB definitional and tabulation changes across editions, plus discontinuation/re-housing of communal-violence reporting between MHA and NCRB, complicate crime and communal-incident trend analysis across 2014.

title: Contested governance indices (RSF, Freedom House, V-Dem)
whatChanged: Third-party democracy/press indices carry their own methodology disputes and periodic recalibrations. Baseline readings circa 2014: RSF rank ~140 (score ~40.3); Freedom House 'Free' (downgrade to 'Partly Free' came 2021); V-Dem liberal-democracy scores higher pre-2014. Recorded as readings, not settled facts; the government contests their methods.

sources.name: RSF World Press Freedom Index archive

title: Peer-country GDP rebasings and WDI vintage drift
whatChanged: Comparator countries revised their own national accounts inside the study window: Vietnam's 2021 rebasing lifted GDP levels ~25%; Bangladesh rebased to 2015-16 with a similar upward level shift. World Bank WDI back-propagates these, so the same query on different dates returns different histories. The peer panel must be pinned to a single WDI vintage, recorded in every series' source.vintage field.
bridgeNote: Pin one WDI vintage for the whole panel; re-pull the entire panel, never one country, when refreshing.
notes: Scoped to 'all': this is a methodological property of every World Bank WDI pull, not a macro-specific one — any domain carrying a peer panel inherits it.

title: Third GDP base-year revision to 2022-23 (released 27 February 2026)
whatChanged: MoSPI released a new national accounts series rebased from 2011-12 to 2022-23, adopting double deflation, a Supply-Use Table framework, and new source data (GST returns, PLFS, ASUSE). It revised recent real growth UP (FY24 8.2%→7.2%, FY25 6.5%→7.1%, FY26 estimated 7.6%) while lowering the LEVEL of nominal GDP by roughly 3-4%. The level cut mechanically RAISES every ratio-to-GDP in the project — deficit, debt, exports, GFCF, tax — without any change in underlying activity. Advisory body: ACNAS, chaired by Prof. Biswanath Goldar. 'Sources and Methods' documentation due August 2026.
bridgeNote: Back-series to be spliced at disaggregated level; not yet published. Until it is, FY24 and FY25 have two valid growth figures and every ratio-to-GDP has two valid denominators. Instrument policy: THREE regimes, never one line.

competingAccounts.position: Routine decadal rebasing to a recent normal post-COVID year; methodologically superior (double deflation, SUT, GST-based data)

A rebasing that simultaneously raises growth and lowers the level arrives conveniently; the absence of published Sources and Methods until Aug 2026 makes independent verification impossible in the interim

sources.name: MoSPI Press Note on New Series of GDP Estimates, base 2022-23

notes: Supersedes the project's original two-regime assumption. CLAUDE.md rule 5 must be amended from 'both GDP series' to 'all three regimes'.

title: CPI base revision to 2024 (new series from February 2026)
whatChanged: A new CPI series with base year 2024 was introduced, with weights redrawn from the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey and a higher non-food weight. Since food inflation drove most headline breaches in 2020 and 2022-23, a lower food weight mechanically dampens future headline volatility relative to the old basket — meaning post-2026 inflation performance is not directly comparable with the 2014-2025 record on which the inflation-targeting verdict rests.
bridgeNote: Weight-effect decomposition would be needed to compare like with like across the break.
notes: Tier-4 sourcing pending a T1 MoSPI press note pull. Flagged in the open verification queue.

title: IIP and WPI base revisions; new Producer Price Index
whatChanged: IIP rebasing to 2022-23 (due around May 2026), a WPI revision in progress, and a planned Producer Price Index. Industrial-production and wholesale-price series will break at these points.

title: Fiscal anchor changes from deficit to debt (from FY2026-27)
whatChanged: From FY27 the Centre shifts its operational fiscal anchor from the annual fiscal-deficit ratio to a debt-to-GDP target (central debt ~56.1% in FY26, glide to 50%±1% by FY31). Fiscal performance before and after FY27 is therefore benchmarked against different objectives. Compounding: P-10 lowered the GDP denominator by 3-4%, which raises measured debt/GDP without any change in borrowing.
bridgeNote: Both measures remain computable; the break is in what counts as success, not in the data.

title: World Bank WDI fiscal-year labelling for India versus calendar years for peers
whatChanged: WDI labels India's fiscal-year observations by the starting calendar year, so WDI '2014' for India corresponds to FY2014-15 (Apr 2014-Mar 2015), while '2014' for Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and China is a different period basis. Peer comparisons drawn straight from WDI therefore compare India's FY with peers' CY, offset by up to nine months — material when a shock (2020 COVID, 2022 commodity spike) lands mid-year. This also explains the apparent conflict between the Phase 1 exports figure (25.4% of GDP, FY2013-14, T1) and WDI's 22.97% for '2014': they are different periods, not contradictory sources.
bridgeNote: State the period basis on every peer chart; never present an India WDI year and a peer WDI year as the same period without the offset noted. VERIFY the WDI India labelling convention against WDI documentation before relying on this record.
notes: Discovered while reconciling Phase 1 and Phase 2 export figures. Convention stated from general knowledge — flagged for primary verification. Scoped to 'all': this is a methodological property of every World Bank WDI pull, not a macro-specific one — any domain carrying a peer panel inherits it.

title: Asset Quality Review recognition break (2015-16)
whatChanged: The RBI's Asset Quality Review forced uniform recognition of stressed accounts previously evergreened through Corporate Debt Restructuring, and withdrew special dispensations for restructured loans. Reported NPA ratios rose steeply as a result of RECOGNITION, not of deterioration: PSB gross NPAs went from 4.97% (Mar 2015) to a peak of 14.58% (Mar 2018). Pre-2015 NPA figures are therefore not comparable with post-AQR figures — the 4.4% recorded at the 2014 handover describes a reporting regime, not an asset quality.
bridgeNote: No official restatement of pre-AQR figures exists. Any chart spanning 2015-16 must mark the break; the rise is not a deterioration event.

competingAccounts.position: Recognition was necessary and overdue; delay would have compounded the eventual cost
Execution was too abrupt and precipitated a credit squeeze — PCA-bank loan books shrank ~11% FY15-FY18, contributing to the pre-COVID slowdown

sources.name: PIB, GNPA of PSBs declined from the peak of 14.58%

notes: Replaces an incorrect reference to P-06 (off-budget borrowing) carried in the phase-1 seed data.

title: COVID-era regulatory forbearance suppressing reported NPAs
whatChanged: The March-August 2020 loan moratorium, the Supreme Court-ordered asset classification standstill, and successive restructuring windows suppressed reported NPA figures through FY2020-21 and FY2021-22. Reported ratios for those years understate underlying stress, and the subsequent decline partly reflects forbearance unwinding rather than a clean trajectory.

title: Write-offs and denominator growth flattering the headline NPA ratio
whatChanged: The fall in the gross NPA ratio from its 2018 peak is driven by three distinct mechanisms that the headline number does not separate: genuine recoveries and upgrades (RBI attributes ~42.8% of the FY2024-25 reduction to these), write-offs (₹16,61,310 crore cumulative April 2014-September 2024, of which only ₹2,69,795 crore — about 16% — was recovered), and rapid credit growth expanding the denominator (domestic credit rose from ₹66.91 to ₹181.34 lakh crore, 2015-2025). The ratio improvement is real but overstates the extent of genuine cleanup.
bridgeNote: Adjusted series = (gross NPA amount + cumulative write-offs) / gross advances, all on the SAME bank population and the SAME reporting basis. REQUIRES: scb-gross-npa-amount, scb-gross-advances, and a cumulative write-off series for the identical population. Currently renderable ONLY for SCB domestic operations at FY2013-14, FY2017-18 and FY2024-25 — the three sourced points. NOT renderable for PSBs: write-offs are all-SCB, so applying them to a PSB ratio mixes populations and describes neither group. NOT renderable as a continuous annual line until an annual advances series is pinned from RBI Trend & Progress. Do not substitute 'domestic credit' for gross advances.

competingAccounts.position: A write-off is an accounting measure that does not extinguish borrower liability; recovery efforts continue on written-off accounts
Recovery on written-off accounts runs at roughly 13-18% in practice, so the distinction is largely notional for the bulk of the amount; depositors and taxpayers absorbed the loss

sources.name: PIB, Building Trust: Strengthening India's banking sector

notes: The single most consequential interpretive issue in the banking domain. Write-off totals derive from RBI RTI responses reported through journalism; the government disputes the interpretation, not the figures.

title: Domestic-operations versus global-operations reporting basis
whatChanged: Indian NPA statistics are published on two bases and official sources mix them without always labelling which is in use. The frequently quoted PSB peak of 14.58% (March 2018) is on the global-operations basis; the scheduled-commercial-bank figure for the same period on domestic operations is 11.46%. Comparing a figure on one basis with a figure on the other produces spurious movements of two to three percentage points.
bridgeNote: Tag every NPA point with its basis. Never compare across bases without conversion.

sources.name: PIB, SCB gross NPAs for domestic operations

title: Risk-weight changes on unsecured retail and NBFC lending (Nov 2023, partial rollback Feb 2025)
whatChanged: In November 2023 the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit from 100% to 125% and added 25 percentage points to bank lending to NBFCs. In February 2025 it partially rolled this back — bank-to-NBFC weights restored effective 1 April 2025 and the microfinance consumer-credit weight cut back to 100% — while retaining 125% on unsecured retail. Capital ratios and unsecured-credit growth series are not comparable across FY2024 to FY2026 without accounting for these changes.

title: RBI fraud reporting: date of occurrence versus date of detection
whatChanged: The RBI is reported to have changed the basis of its fraud statistics from date of detection to date of occurrence, which materially changes year-on-year fraud totals and reassigns large historical frauds to earlier years. Any fraud time series spanning the change is not comparable.
bridgeNote: The change is asserted across multiple secondary sources but the primary RBI circular and its effective date have NOT been located. Do not publish any fraud time series until this is pinned.

sources.name: Secondary reporting, pending primary RBI notification

notes: Highest-priority verification item from this cycle. This record is provisional.

title: Expected Credit Loss provisioning transition (from 1 April 2027)
whatChanged: RBI final directions issued 27 April 2026 mandate a shift from incurred-loss to expected-credit-loss provisioning effective 1 April 2027, with a glide path to March 2031. Estimated one-time capital impact is around 60-70 basis points system-wide, larger for banks with heavy unsecured or microfinance exposure. Provisioning coverage and reported asset-quality figures after FY2027 will not be directly comparable with prior years.
bridgeNote: A forward-dated break. Set a re-baselining trigger for FY2027-28 data.
